summary: Psalm 61 begins as a cry from an overwhelmed heart asking God to hear and lead the speaker to safety. The prayer recalls God as refuge, asks for lasting shelter, then turns toward the king’s preservation and ends with a promise of ongoing praise and fulfilled vows.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how a short prayer can move from personal distress to trust, royal hope, and public praise. Within Book II of Psalms, it is one more David-associated poem where danger is answered by appeal to God’s protection rather than by explanation of the crisis.

context.author: The heading says “By David,” but Psalms’ headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or collection; readers differ on how much the heading establishes historically.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, with later Jewish and Christian readers also adopting the psalm as prayer.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 61 is uncertain.
context.setting: The speaker feels far away and overwhelmed, while the poem’s images look toward God’s tent, shelter, and the king before God.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew prayer poetry with a musical heading, compressed images of refuge, and a movement from plea to praise.

outline.heading: A Cry For Hearing
outline.note: The psalm opens with a musical heading and a direct request that God hear and listen.

outline.heading: Overwhelmed But Calling
outline.note: From a place described as “the end of the earth,” the speaker asks to be led to a higher rock.

outline.heading: Remembered Refuge
outline.note: The prayer grounds its request in God’s past protection and seeks lasting shelter in God’s tent and wings.

outline.heading: Vows And Heritage
outline.note: The speaker says God has heard the vows and given a heritage among those who fear God’s name.

outline.heading: Prayer For The King
outline.note: The psalm asks that the king’s life and reign be preserved by God’s loving kindness and truth.

outline.heading: Praise Continued Daily
outline.note: The poem closes with a promise to sing praise and fulfill vows day by day.

keyVerses.text: From the end of the earth, I will call to you when my heart is overwhelmed. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the psalm’s central pressure: distance, an overwhelmed heart, and the need for God to lead the speaker to safety beyond personal reach.

keyVerses.text: For you have been a refuge for me, a strong tower from the enemy.
keyVerses.why: The prayer asks for help on the basis of remembered protection, using two of the chapter’s main refuge images.

keyVerses.text: He shall be enthroned in God’s presence forever. Appoint your loving kindness and truth, that they may preserve him.
keyVerses.why: This verse turns the psalm’s trust toward the king, asking that God’s own qualities preserve him.

keyVerses.text: So I will sing praise to your name forever, that I may fulfill my vows daily.
keyVerses.why: The final line shows where the prayer is headed: continuing praise and faithful completion of vows.

themes: God as refuge and strong tower

questions.question: What is happening in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter does not describe a specific event. It gives the words of a speaker who feels overwhelmed and far away, asks God to hear, remembers God’s past protection, prays for the king, and promises continuing praise.

questions.question: Does “By David” prove David wrote every line?
questions.answer: The heading associates the psalm with David. Psalm headings are ancient features of the Psalter, but the wording can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, so readers differ on how definite the claim is.

questions.question: What does “For the Chief Musician. For a stringed instrument” mean?
questions.answer: The opening line preserves a performance heading. It points to musical use, but the ancient melodies and the exact force of some performance terms are no longer known.

questions.question: What does “from the end of the earth” mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase expresses the speaker’s sense of distance while still calling to God. The chapter does not say whether this is literal geography, emotional estrangement, exile-like language, or poetic exaggeration, so it is best to keep the image open.

questions.question: What is the “rock that is higher than I”?
questions.answer: The line asks God to lead the speaker to a place of security beyond the speaker’s own ability to reach. In the chapter’s imagery, it belongs with refuge, strong tower, tent, and wings as pictures of protection.

questions.question: Is the speaker asking to live in a literal tent forever?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says, “I will dwell in your tent forever,” and then adds the image of taking refuge under God’s wings. The chapter uses shelter language to express nearness and protection with God; it does not explain the exact physical setting behind the image.

questions.question: Who is “the king” in verses 6-7?
questions.answer: The poem moves from “I” to a prayer for “the king.” In its first literary setting this points to royal hope within Israel’s prayer, while later Jewish and Christian readers may hear broader messianic significance; those later readings should not erase the chapter’s immediate royal language.

questions.question: What are the “vows” in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter mentions vows twice: God has heard them, and the speaker intends to fulfill them daily. It does not specify their content, but it connects them with received heritage and ongoing praise.

questions.question: How should a first-time reader follow the movement of the chapter?
questions.answer: Read it as a short movement from request to remembered trust to renewed commitment. The speaker begins by asking God to listen, names the overwhelmed heart, recalls God’s protection, asks for the king’s preservation, and ends with daily praise.

glossary.def: A phrase in the heading that marks the psalm for musical or worship use, though the exact ancient role is not explained in the chapter.
The heading’s musical direction; it tells the reader the psalm was connected with instrumental performance.
A preserved performance marker in verse 4. Its exact instruction is uncertain, so many translations leave the word as it stands.
Promises or commitments made before God. In this psalm they have been heard by God and are to be fulfilled daily.
A quality the speaker asks God to appoint for the king’s preservation, paired in verse 7 with truth.
